strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and well-motivated limitation of prior GRF methods (Choromanski 2023; Reid et al. 2023/2024): the inherently sequential nature of long random walks limits both computational efficiency and expressiveness for distant node pairs. The walk-stitching idea (concatenating shorter, parallelizable walks while preserving unbiasedness) is a clean and non-trivial technical contribution.

Solid theoretical backing: the paper proves unbiasedness of the stitching mechanism under a general termination scheme (Lemma 3.1, generalizing Lemma 2.1), derives a closed-form MSE expression for degree l=2 (Lemma 3.2), and proves a monotonic-improvement result for degrees that are powers of two (Theorem 3.3). Proofs are included in the appendix and appear rigorous.

The generalized termination strategy (replacing the fixed Bernoulli halting scheme with arbitrary discrete distributions, e.g., Poisson) is a nice, low-cost extension that is shown empirically to improve accuracy at no extra parallel-compute cost.

Broad and diverse empirical evaluation: kernel approximation error across 8 graphs of varying size/topology, accuracy specifically on long-diameter graphs (Peptides, CIFAR, Reddit-Binary, GeometricShapes, etc.), and three downstream tasks (graph classification, node clustering, mesh vertex-normal prediction) with consistent gains over regular GRFs and near-parity with the exact (brute-force) kernel.

Useful ablation isolating the specific contribution of walk-stitching by re-using the exact same underlying random walks as the GRF baseline, which cleanly disentangles the stitching mechanism's benefit from sampling more walks.
Reasonably detailed reproducibility/appendix material: hyperparameter choices, dataset statistics, and mesh IDs are all specified, aiding replication even though code is not yet released.
weaknesses: The wall-clock speed comparison (Fig. 5, 'Computational Time') is not fully convincing: it reports 'Walk Time' and 'Stitching Time' separately decreasing with degree, but does not clearly present total end-to-end runtime versus baseline GRFs on real parallel hardware, nor discuss how well the claimed GPU parallelism is actually realized in practice (e.g., wall-clock latency under batched GPU execution vs. CPU sequential simulation).

Theorem 3.3 (monotonic MSE improvement) is only proven for degrees that are powers of two, leaving open whether monotonic improvement holds for general stitching degree l, which is a gap between the theoretical claim and the practically used range of degrees (2-6) shown in the experiments.

The overhead of the general termination strategy (computing tail probabilities τ(k)=P(X≥k) for arbitrary distributions, needed in the modified update rule) is not analyzed; this could offset some of the claimed 'no extra computational cost' benefit for distributions where τ(k) is not cheap to compute.

Novelty is somewhat incremental relative to the existing GRF literature (Choromanski 2023; Reid et al. 2023, 2024a, 2024b): the core idea is essentially a convolution/factorization trick for combining GRF outputs, and the significance is fairly specialized to the graph-kernel-approximation community rather than broader ML.

Presentation is dense in places, particularly the matrix bookkeeping for Option I/II/III (Eqs. 5-7) and the notation-heavy proofs, which may hinder accessibility; some notation (e.g., mixing p and t as walk-length variables, overloaded X/Y symbols) could be streamlined.
Code is not released with the submission (promised only upon acceptance), which somewhat limits immediate reproducibility despite the otherwise detailed methodological description.

No comparison against alternative long-range kernel approximation strategies outside the GRF family (e.g., sparse iterative solvers, other random-feature or low-rank approximation techniques), making it hard to judge how GRFs++ stacks up against the broader landscape of scalable graph kernel computation methods.

strengths: The core idea of walk-stitching—concatenating several independently-sampled short random walks instead of sampling one long walk—is a sensible and reasonably novel way to trade sequential sampling for parallelizable matrix-matrix operations, and is well-motivated by hardware/accelerator considerations.

The paper provides a non-trivial theoretical foundation: a general unbiasedness proof for walk-stitching combined with arbitrary termination distributions (Lemma 3.1/App. A.1), a closed-form MSE expression for degree l=2 (Lemma 3.2), and a monotonic-improvement result (Theorem 3.3).

The generalization of walk termination from fixed-probability Bernoulli schemes to arbitrary discrete distributions (e.g., Poisson) is a clean, easily implementable extension that is shown empirically to help.

Experimental coverage is broad: kernel-approximation accuracy on 8+ graphs, long-diameter graphs from several benchmark datasets, three downstream tasks (classification, clustering, mesh normal prediction), and an ablation re-using the same walks to isolate the stitching effect.
Reproducibility is reasonably addressed: algorithms are given in full detail, datasets and hyperparameter ranges are specified, and proofs are included in the appendix.
weaknesses: Theorem 3.3, the main theoretical justification that increasing the walk-stitching degree always helps, is only proved for degrees that are powers of two (1,2,4,8,...) and only under the 'standard' Bernoulli termination strategy; the paper's broader claims about general l and general termination distributions are not backed by a matching formal guarantee.

The computational-efficiency claims are not substantiated with a clear, direct wall-clock comparison of total end-to-end time (walk + stitching) between GRFs++ and regular GRFs across degrees; Fig. 5 only shows the two components separately and is hard to parse quantitatively from the text, leaving the central efficiency claim (parallel short walks being cheaper overall) only weakly supported.

The empirical comparison is narrow: the only baseline is regular (vanilla) GRFs; there is no comparison to other graph-kernel approximation or random-feature techniques (e.g., Nystrom-style low-rank approximations, quasi-MC GRFs, repelling random walks, or spectral sketches) that could contextualize how large the practical gain really is.

Gains from increasing the walk-stitching degree appear to show diminishing/marginal returns beyond degree 2–3 in several figures (Figs. 2–4), raising doubts about the practical significance of the more general l>2 machinery relative to its added complexity.

Downstream task results are mixed in their strength of support for the central claims: graph classification results are described as merely 'on par' with the exact diffusion kernel baseline rather than a clear improvement, weakening the case that the more accurate kernel approximation translates into better downstream performance.

The choice of the Poisson termination distribution is presented largely as an empirical choice without a principled derivation of why it (or any particular family) is a good or optimal choice relative to other general termination distributions satisfying the stated mild assumptions.

Presentation is dense and notation-heavy (e.g., Eq. 4, Eq. 16-18), with several claims (e.g., 'no extra computational cost', 'improves estimation accuracy') stated confidently in the main text before being fully qualified or justified in the appendix, risking overstatement of the generality of the results.

strengths: The walk-stitching mechanism is a genuinely novel and well-motivated idea: it resolves the sequential bottleneck of long random walks in regular GRFs by combining short, parallelizable walks while provably preserving unbiasedness (Lemma 2.1/3.1), and it directly addresses the long-standing GRF weakness of poor coverage of distant node pairs.

Solid theoretical backbone: unbiasedness proof for the generalized termination scheme (Lemma 3.1, Appendix A.1), a clean closed-form MSE expression for degree l=2 (Lemma 3.2, Appendix A.2), and a monotonic improvement result for powers-of-two degrees (Theorem 3.3, Appendix A.3) with full proofs provided.

The generalization of the walk termination mechanism from fixed-probability Bernoulli trials to arbitrary discrete distributions (e.g., Poisson) is simple to implement, maintains unbiasedness, and is shown empirically to improve accuracy at no extra cost (Fig. 3).

Connects the walk-stitching construction to a nice, interpretable algorithmic recipe based on (2l)-th root/de-convolution of the kernel-generating function, giving closed-form modulation functions for practically relevant kernels like the diffusion kernel.

Thorough empirical validation across many axes: approximation accuracy vs. number of walks on 8 graphs of varied structure/size, accuracy on large-diameter graphs from diverse domains (Peptides, CIFAR, Reddit-Binary, GeometricShapes), wall-clock speed breakdown, and three downstream tasks (graph classification, node clustering, mesh normal prediction) with consistent gains over baseline GRFs.

Useful ablation isolating the walk-stitching effect from the effect of additional random walks (Fig. 4, reusing identical walks across degrees), strengthening the causal claim that stitching itself (not just more sampling) drives the improvement.
weaknesses: The general-l MSE analysis is only worked out for the special case l=2; the paper admits the general formula is "complicated" and does not provide it, and Theorem 3.3 only proves monotonic improvement for degrees restricted to powers of two, leaving the behavior for arbitrary l theoretically unresolved.

Reported wall-clock timing experiments (Fig. 5) are limited to a single synthetic setting (500-node random graphs) and do not include comparisons against stronger/competing acceleration baselines (e.g., JLT-based low-rank GRFs, or exact kernel computation crossover points), making the practical efficiency claims only partially substantiated.

No released code at submission time (promised only upon acceptance), which limits independent verification of implementation details such as the construction of the stitched matrices X, Y and the general termination-strategy modification (Algorithm 2), despite otherwise clear algorithmic descriptions.

Guidance on selecting the key hyperparameters in practice (stitching degree l, termination distribution P) is largely empirical/ad hoc (grid search over small sets), with no principled method or adaptive scheme suggested, which could limit usability for practitioners.

Graphs used in most accuracy experiments are relatively small (up to ~1300 nodes, aside from mesh/classification datasets), so scalability of the O(N^2) matrix-matrix multiplication-based construction to very large graphs is not empirically demonstrated.

The paper lacks an explicit, dedicated limitations/discussion section; potential failure modes (e.g., when stitching degree is too high relative to graph diameter, or when kernel de-convolution lacks a simple closed form) are not systematically discussed.

strengths: The paper introduces two well-motivated extensions to Graph Random Features (GRFs): a walk-stitching mechanism that composes short random walks (amenable to parallel/matrix computation) to emulate long walks, and a generalized walk-termination scheme beyond the Bernoulli halting rule. Both are non-trivial generalizations addressing genuine, previously identified weaknesses of GRFs (sequential sampling cost, poor modeling of distant-node relationships).

Solid theoretical grounding: unbiasedness is proven in a fairly general setting (Lemma 2.1/3.1, connecting the construction to higher-order de-convolutions of the kernel's generating function), a closed-form MSE expression is derived for degree l=2 (Lemma 3.2), and a monotonic improvement result with stitching degree is shown (Theorem 3.3), with detailed proofs in the appendix.

Very extensive empirical evaluation: kernel approximation accuracy across 8+ synthetic/real graphs, targeted analysis of long-distance node pairs on large-diameter graphs, ablations isolating the walk-stitching effect from walk reuse, wall-clock speed comparisons against brute-force kernel construction on large meshes, and four diverse downstream tasks (ViT attention masking, graph classification, node clustering, mesh normal prediction) plus integration into GraphGPS/Performer. Results are consistently favorable for GRFs++ relative to regular GRFs.
Reasonable reproducibility effort: hyperparameters, dataset statistics, and experimental protocols are documented in the appendix, and the authors state they will open-source code.
weaknesses: Theorem 3.3 (accuracy improves monotonically with stitching degree) is only proven for degrees that are powers of two, yet the abstract/intro imply a general benefit of increasing stitching degree; the gap between the general claim and the restricted proof is not clearly flagged in the main text.

The paper empirically recommends reusing the same set of random walks across the l components of GRFs++ (breaking the independence assumption required for unbiasedness), reporting this 'performs well in practice,' but provides no theoretical characterization of the resulting bias or its magnitude — this is an important practical deviation from the proven guarantees that is under-analyzed.

Several experimental choices (e.g., fixing stitching degree l=2 for most downstream tasks, hyperparameter sweeps for baselines vs. proposed method) are not deeply justified, and it is unclear how sensitive results are to these choices or how they were selected (risk of some selection favoring the proposed method).

In the graph classification comparisons, the paper acknowledges its kernel is an intra-graph (node) kernel while most baselines are inter-graph kernels, making the 'competitive performance' claims only loosely comparable; the practical significance of this comparison is therefore limited.

Presentation is dense in places, with some inconsistent notation across sections (e.g., ξρ(i) in Algorithm 1 vs. φf(i)/ϕf(i) in the text, and K1^(i) vs. K_1^i indexing), which could hinder reproducibility for a reader trying to precisely align the algorithm boxes with the theoretical statements.
The Impact Statement is essentially boilerplate and does not meaningfully engage with any potential limitations or societal implications specific to this work.

strengths: Addresses two genuine and well-known limitations of Graph Random Features (GRFs): the inherently sequential, hard-to-parallelize sampling of long walks, and the simplistic Bernoulli-only termination scheme. The proposed walk-stitching mechanism and generalized termination strategy are conceptually sound ideas with a clear connection to higher-order deconvolutions of the kernel-generating function.

Solid theoretical backbone: unbiasedness is proven for the general walk-stitching + general-termination setting (Lemma 3.1), a closed-form MSE expression is derived for degree l=2 (Lemma 3.2), and a monotonic improvement result is shown for degrees that are powers of two (Theorem 3.3), with full proofs provided in the appendix.

Very broad empirical validation spanning kernel-approximation accuracy on 8 graphs, long-diameter/distant-node estimation, a novel Poisson-termination ablation, runtime/scalability comparisons against brute-force computation, and four distinct downstream applications (ViT attention masking, graph classification, node clustering, mesh normal-vector prediction) plus integration into GraphGPS/Performer, which collectively give a reasonably convincing picture that the method is practically useful, not just theoretically interesting.

Reasonable reproducibility effort: algorithms are given in full pseudocode, all datasets/graph-generation procedures are specified, hyperparameter sweeps are described, and the authors state they will open-source the implementation.
weaknesses: The fairness of the core accuracy comparisons (Fig. 2, 3, 9–11) is unclear: GRFs++ of degree l requires constructing l independent pairs of K1/K2 matrices, implying a walk budget that scales with l, yet the x-axis is simply labeled 'number of random walks m' without clarifying whether this equalizes total sampled walks/compute across degrees. Without a compute- or walk-count-matched comparison, the reported accuracy gains for higher degree l could partly reflect a larger effective sampling budget rather than a genuinely better estimator per unit of parallel/serial work.

The claimed preservation of sparsity for Option I ('If all the matrices K_j^(i) are sparse... then X, Y can be computed in O(N^2) for constant l and are also sparse') is asserted but not rigorously justified; products of sparse matrices (even with linear nonzeros each) can densify quickly as l grows, which is central to the paper's efficiency argument but is not analyzed quantitatively or verified empirically (e.g., via reported nonzero counts after stitching).

Theorem 3.3, the main result showing improvement from stitching, is only proven for degrees restricted to powers of two and under the 'standard termination strategy,' leaving the monotonicity claim for arbitrary l and for the newly proposed general termination schemes unestablished.

Several downstream results report small absolute gains (e.g., ImageNet 80.10→80.31, Places365 55.78→56.03, several graph-classification datasets with <1.5 point differences) without confidence intervals, significance tests, or multiple seeds, making it hard to judge whether the improvements are meaningful versus noise.

The method presentation is dense and notation-heavy (three 'Options', multiple algorithm variants, degree-parity case splits in Eq. 5–6), which hurts readability and could be streamlined; the paper would benefit from a unifying pseudocode for the full (l, P)-GRFs++ procedure rather than scattered prose descriptions.

No comparison against other efficient/alternative approaches to long-range graph kernel approximation beyond the authors' own prior GRF work (e.g., Nyström-type methods, other random-walk truncation or control-variate techniques), limiting the ability to contextualize the significance of the proposed gains relative to the broader literature.
The impact statement is essentially boilerplate and does not meaningfully engage with any potential considerations specific to the work.

strengths: The paper addresses two concrete, well-motivated limitations of regular Graph Random Features (GRFs): (1) difficulty capturing long-range node relationships without sampling long, sequential walks, and (2) a restrictive Bernoulli walk-termination scheme. The proposed walk-stitching mechanism and generalized termination strategy are both intuitive and technically grounded.

Strong theoretical backing: unbiasedness of the walk-stitching estimator is proven in generality (Lemma 2.1/3.1), a closed-form MSE expression is derived for degree-2 stitching (Lemma 3.2), and a monotonic improvement result for powers-of-two stitching degree is proven (Theorem 3.3). The connection to higher-order de-convolutions of the kernel's generating function is a nice conceptual contribution that also yields practical closed-form modulation functions (e.g., for diffusion kernels).

Extensive empirical validation across many axes: approximation accuracy vs. number of walks on 8 graphs, long-distance kernel estimation on large-diameter graphs (diameter up to 159), a novel Poisson termination strategy, computational speed/scalability comparisons (including against brute-force on meshes up to 35K nodes), and four downstream tasks (image classification via ViT masking, graph classification, node clustering, mesh normal prediction), plus integration into GraphGPS. This breadth strongly supports the generality of the claimed benefits.

The method preserves key practical properties of regular GRFs (sparsity, parallelizability, sub-quadratic complexity) while enabling parallel computation of short walks instead of sequential long-walk sampling, which is a genuine systems-level advantage for modern hardware.

The ablation re-using the same random walks across stitching components (Fig. 5a) is a useful practical finding, even though it sacrifices strict unbiasedness, and the paper is transparent about this trade-off.
The paper is generally well organized, with proofs deferred to the appendix and a dedicated reproducibility statement describing algorithmic specification and dataset/experimental details.
weaknesses: The claimed closed-form MSE monotonicity result (Theorem 3.3) is only proven for degrees that are powers of two, and the general-l MSE formula is stated to be "complicated" without being given; it is unclear how the method behaves/compares for arbitrary l, which is what is actually used in several experiments (e.g., up to degree 6 in Fig. 2).

Computational complexity claims are somewhat informally stated (e.g., "for constant l" assumptions throughout Sec. 2.2.3) without a precise big-O characterization of how stitching degree l trades off against walk length/accuracy, making it hard to assess the true efficiency-accuracy Pareto frontier compared to regular GRFs with shorter walks and larger m.

The experimental gains, while consistent, are often fairly small in absolute terms for several downstream tasks (e.g., ImageNet top-1: 80.10 vs 80.31; node clustering and graph classification gains are also modest), raising questions about practical significance despite statistical/empirical consistency.

The paper does not report variance/confidence intervals for many of the downstream task tables (e.g., Tables 1, 2, 3, 4, 5), making it difficult to assess the statistical significance of the reported improvements, especially given the small margins.

The re-using-random-walks trick (shown empirically beneficial, Fig. 5a) technically breaks the independence assumption required for unbiasedness, but this is not theoretically analyzed—only empirically justified—leaving a gap between the theory and what is actually used in several experiments for computational efficiency.

No explicit code/artifact URL is provided in the reviewed manuscript text itself (the reproducibility statement references open-sourcing but no concrete link appears in the submission), which limits immediate reproducibility verification.

The graph classification comparison against the broad kernel/GNN literature (Tables 8, 9, 12) is somewhat apples-to-oranges, as the authors themselves note GRF++ computes intra-graph (node) kernels rather than inter-graph kernels, making some of the positioning relative to prior work a bit misleading despite the caveat.
